and I also know that our Government will do its utmost to prevent similar tragedies from happening again.

Mr. Speaker, last weekend in my riding, I met with two senior citizens groups-one from Temiscamingue and one from Saint-Eugene-de-Guigues.
I can assure the House that the mood during these meetings was very positive and that discussions took place in a relaxed and friendly atmosphere. Mr. Speaker, when we take the time to sit down with them and speak intelligently and without rhetoric, senior citizens understand.
They understand that our Government is struggling with a gigantic deficit that might become a threat to social programs in the future. They understand that the deficit is a national responsibility and that we must all do our fair share. They understand that between now and January 1986, nothing will change and that their cheques will increase from month to month. They also understand that the Budget clearly says that if one of these measures proves to be inequitable, our Government will take corrective action immediately.
Mr. Speaker, in the passionate and extreme kind of debate we are seeing today, the elderly are showing a wisdom that many Members in this House would do well to emulate.

Mr. Speaker, western Canadians are becoming increasingly apprehensive over the recruiting practices of the RCMP. Five per cent of the force is stationed in Quebec, a province which has its own provincial police. Yet in 1983-84 more than half of our RCMP recruits were from Quebec. On the other hand, approximately one half the entire force is employed by the four western provinces which pay the RCMP to provide provincial policing. In 1983-84 only 11 per cent of our recruits came from the West.
Hundreds of young western Canadians are on a list, still hoping to realize their life's ambition of joining the force. Some have been waiting up to four years for a call after having been told, and I quote: "Your name is on the National Waiting List consisting of people who will, in due course, be engaged . .." It is time for the RCMP either to change its engagement practices or to come clean, be honest, and tell these western Canadians there is no place for them.
Surely the RCMP can have a reasonable engagement policy which, while recognizing the new emphasis on special language, university, and other skills, can still fairly reflect the input of the regions in which the force is utilized. A responsible policy ought not to exclude an entire generation of young western Canadians from serving in this proud institution.

Mr. Speaker, "Man in Motion" is not only the theme of Expo 86 but of a unique venture of an outstanding Canadian, Rick Hansen. The opposition Parties did not support with any enthusiasm at all the setting up of the subcommittee. I am glad they have now discovered that it is a valuable exercise, and I hope that by the end of September the committee will have had sufficient time to give us its report. We are prepared to extend it to the end of September, and then we want to take action on these pressing matters that you wanted us to take action on months ago.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Agriculture. Hearings on Bill C-25 concluded last Thursday. Over the weekend livestock producers in western Canada, particularly in Alberta, expressed to me their concern over amendments made to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. There appears to be a wide degree of interpretation of the amendments. Has the Minister received communications from his provincial counterparts and industry spokesmen, and what measures is he taking in addressing these concerns?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome the opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member's question. I want to indicate to him that I have received messages, and telexes from the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I am really concerned about the fact that there is a great deal of misunderstanding and a great deal of misinterpretation about the intent of the amendment.
This amendment does not back away from top-loading. This amendment recognizes the reality of today. This amendment allows us to deal with all market distortions in the industry.
I challenge the provinces, and I challenge the farm leaders and the producers to come together, to sit down around the table and to work together on something that will provide mid and long-term benefits to Canadian agriculture across the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He will know that the Ontario Federation of Agriculture passed a resolution at an
Oral Questions
emergency meeting recently which condemned the Budget for having betrayed the farmers of Canada. It has totally ignored the consultation process and has ignored the legitimate needs of farmers across the country. I want to ask the Minister, since he seems to be in a conciliatory mood, if he is willing to bring in new budget measures providing for long-term low interest rate agri-bonds as his Party promised in the election campaign, and as was recommended by the finance committee of this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, can set these out in more complete terms than I can. There are a number of promises that we made in the campaign that are highlighted in the note that he has just released, that I am sure the Hon. Member, as well as the Ontario Federation of Agriculture would like to see, setting out the number of promises that have been kept.
For instance, we said we would do something on capital gains on farms. We said we would do something on the farm fuel taxes and we put a rebate there that gave the farmers $150 million. We said we would make changes in the metric system, of great help to farmers. I could go on and on, but I believe the Hon. Minister of Agricultre could give a fuller answer on that.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance had read his own Budget well enough he would know that the only provision in the Budget is to help farmers get off the farm, and there are already too many foreclosures taking place. The Minister mentioned reducing the excise tax by 9 per cent last fall-by 10 per cent actually-but in his Budget-
Order, please. This is becoming a preamble. Is there a question, please?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I am just getting there. I wonder, in view of the fact that the Budget does provide for a 9 cents a gallon excise tax to start the first of September, would he give an exemption to farmers and not impose this so-called harvest tax just at the beginning of the fall harvest.
Mr. Speaker, let me tell the Hon. Member about some of the other things that I did not mention in my first answer. We dropped the interest rate on the Farm Credit-
Oh, oh!

They do not like to hear the good news. We dropped the interest rate on Farm Credit Corporation loans from 16.25 per cent to, I believe, 12.75 per cent. Interest rates have gone down during the same period of

June 26, 1985
Oral Questions
time, providing help to all farmers. The price of gasoline for farmers is going down as well. I think the farmers have a lot for which to be thankful because of the very progressive policies that have been followed by this Government, led by my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport a couple of questions. Several months ago the Union of Canadian Transport Employees warned the Government that continued cut-backs and delays would jeopardize safety and security on the ground and in the air, so 75 new fire trucks were ordered for which money was made available over two years ago. The Government seems to be having some difficulty in taking delivery of those fire trucks, and this lowers the standards of the firefighting service one of two grades below the standards set by the Minister's own Department. Can the Minister tell me what the problem is with obtaining delivery of those 75 new fire trucks? I hope it is not because they are painted Liberal red rather than Tory blue.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to advise the Hon. Member that Canada has one of the very highest standards of crash firefighting and prevention services in the world. It is certainly higher than that of Australia and the United States. With respect to the specific question, there may have been a re-profiling of funding, but I am not aware of any outright cancellation as the Hon. Member suggests.

Mr. Speaker, we are faced with the possibility of 109 of the Minister's firefighting branch employees being laid off while he horses around with trucks. In the matter of the investigation that is being carried on, will he tell us who is making it-
Order.
I am not referring to the disaster of last weekend.
Order, please. The Hon. Member has been recognized on a supplementary question presumably with regard to fire trucks.
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister if this investigation will be independent, and if its terms of reference will be broad enough to include safety and security, including fire trucks-
With respect, I appreciate that it is an important question but it is not a supplementary one.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Chairman of the Special Committee on Equality Rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I would ask the Chairman if the committee will hear evidence with respect to the way senior citizens who approach 71 and hold Registered Retirement Savings Certificates are treated by the Income Tax Act and the way they are forced because of age, as no other Canadians are, to buy annuities from an insurance company or enter into Registered Investment Retirement Funds.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In the May 23 Budget the Minister of Finance announced that, as of July 1, a number of new sales taxes will go into effect, so consumers in general, and particularly pensioners, will see their purchasing power reduced, thus putting many of them living under the poverty line. How can the Minister of Finance say that his Budget is fair and helps small business when the new sales tax and the sales tax increase will reduce small business activities, thus reducing the number of new jobs created?

Mr. Speaker, the people representing the small business community, whether they are senior spokespeople from the industry or individuals who work in the small business community, are all very, very supportive of the thrust of the Budget as well as the details of it, after taking everything into account. I think that what the Hon. Member is suggesting is wrong.
I would remind the Hon. Member that Members on his side of the House were saying that the small business community was going to fold up and die as a result of the action taken on November 8. Since then there have been 150,000 jobs created by the small business community. Again, members of the opposition Parties are going around with little black clouds over their heads and are saying that the sky is going to fall in,
June 26, 1985

and that everything will go the wrong way, when actions are proving that everything is going the right way.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very good example of how members of the Opposition are both sucking and blowing. I would ask the Hon. subsubtopic: STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER ON DELIVERY OF SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Is it still the Minister's view, as he has stated to both the Canadian Hospital Association and the provincial Ministers of Health, that the health care system should look to private funding to maintain the level of services Canadians currently enjoy?

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member asked that question because I think that that is not the interpretation that should be placed on this particular discussion. For instance, there are services in hospitals which have been privatized, like laundry services.
Oral Questions
When the Hon. Member and members of the press hear the word "privatization", I do not think that they should draw the long bow by thinking that hospitals as such would be privatized.
Mr. Speaker, muddling through what appears to be a quite convoluted answer, may I ask the Minister directly-

These are Bills with respect to which we received indication that we would be able to get through third reading on these items of legislation.

The two Bills I mentioned fit into that category. Other Bills include the Bill with respect to the sale of the Northern Transportation Company Limited, which I understand is to be reported back to the House today from the Standing Committee on Transport.
I believe there would be a disposition to complete consideration of third reading of that legislation so that the Senate may also pass it and so that it may receive Royal Assent.

There have also been discussions with respect to other items of legislation, such as a Bill which increases the number of judges in certain provinces at the request of the provinces. It is a non-controversial Bill, I believe. I hope there will be a disposition to deal with that Bill at all stages in the House so that the Senate could also pass it.
As well, Mr. Speaker, we have had discussions on the amendments to Standing Orders to bring into effect the recommendations of the first report of the Standing Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons at the beginning of September. I think we have a consensus among House Leaders with respect to that process.
There will be an amendment to the House of Commons Act, Mr. Speaker, which will create, in accordance with the recommendations of the Standing Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, the new Board of Internal Economy effective September 9, 1985.
These are some of the items of which I have given a list and would want to have passed before we adjourn. before Hon. Members can consider going on summer recess. We hope to do that by this Friday. However, I leave that in the hands of members of the Opposition. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) rose on a point of order to ask the Chair to review the proceedings of the House on June 20, 1985, on Motion No. 7 of Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Aeronautics Act at report stage. I have his request and have examined the record.
The Hon. Member is correct in noting that the Votes and Proceedings do not reflect the sequence of events. However, I would refer him to Citation 149, paragraph 1 of the Fifth Edition of Beauchesne's which states that the Votes and Proceedings record all that is or-and I underline the "or"-is deemed to be done by the House. During consideration of the motion standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), and subsequently, the House was operating under unusual circumstances in that there was unanimous consent to revert back to report stage and have the motion, which had in fact been carried, rescinded. The record shows that the motion was negatived. Again, I remind the Hon. Members, as indicated by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), that all of this was done by unanimous consent and, after Motion No. 7 was negatived, the House continued with debate on third reading. To have recorded all of this process in the Votes and Proceedings would have resulted in a very confusing record of the proceedings and would have provided in fact more information than was required to record the final decision of the House. He said: Mr. Speaker, I took note of your remarks earlier with reference to the Class of '68. I would just like to utilize this opportunity to congratulate those people who were victorious, from all Parties, of course. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I well recall the year 1968 back in my riding of Elgin. Good fortune did not come our way in the riding of Elgin back in 1968. Two things happened on that day back in 1968, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Advance Payments for Crops Act Speaker, first, it rained torrents from early morning until late night and, second, when the ballots were counted, our Party ended up with the short stick. So the good days in the riding of Elgin did not take place for us until the election of October, 1972.
On my travels across Canada, Mr. Speaker, in the past several months, I have been asked by many farmers and farm organizations if and when the federal Government would bring forth legislation to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act. They told me it is a good program but it is out of date. It is based on farming costs and commodity prices from almost a decade ago. My answer to those people has always been "very soon". Well, Mr. Speaker, "soon" is right now, before our deliberations end for the summer.
It is in this regard today that I want to introduce for second reading a Bill to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act. Before discussing the proposed amendments, I should first remind the House what the Advance Payments for Crops Program is all about. The object of the program is to assist in the orderly marketing of agricultural crops in all parts of Canada. It does this, as the title implies, by advancing interest free payments to producers for storable crops prior to harvest time. This gives producers the financial flexibility to market their crops over the full marketing season when returns are normally higher than at harvest time. When the crop is sold, the money is repaid to the federal Government. In other words, this program provides farmers with some cash to see them through the period from planting time to the time they are able to sell their crop. In the case of some crops, that can be many, many months. Consider, for instance, the British Columbia apple, the Ontario rutabagas and the Prince Edward Island potatoes which are in the stores now. They were not harvested in June, 1985. They probably came out of the field in September, 1984. Where have they been for the past nine months? Most likely they were not sitting in a supermarket or a wholesaler's warehouse. They were probably stored in farm cold storages across the country. In all that time the producer was not paid unless, of course, he received an advance payment under the very Act which I propose that we amend today.
There have been no changes made to this piece of legislation since it was enacted in 1977. It is now time to amend this Act in order to optimize its marketing potential. The first amendment would double the maximum level of advance payments allowed under the Act in any crop year from $15,000 to $30,000 per individual producer, and from $30,000 and $45,000 for business organizations to $60,000 and $90,000. Under an Appropriation Act, these levels could be raised to amounts fixed by Parliament.
This amendment would bring the maximum advance levels in line with those under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Program. The present inequities between the two programs has caused confusion among producers concerning the two programs in western Canada. Understandably, producer organizations have been asking Agriculture Canada to eliminate these inequities.
The present maximum levels under the Advance Payments for Crops Act were set in 1977. Over the past eight years, producers' input costs have risen at a much faster rate than their market returns. Thus, a smaller portion of the producer's crop is now covered by the program. Over the past eight years producer input costs have risen at a much higher rate than market returns. Thus, a smaller portion of the producers' crop is now covered by the program. This has reduced the producers' marketing flexibility and therefore his return. But amending the advanced levels will serve no purpose unless the total size of the program is increased. For each of the past three years the total guaranteed amounts approach the present $200 million maximum contingent liability. Thus, this legislation doubles the Government's contingent liability from $200 million to $400 million.
It is only reasonable that the size of the program should double since there is increased interest in it by producers and producer organizations. They see the advance payments for crops program as one which helps them to lengthen the marketing season for storable crops, improves their cash flow positions, and helps defend against variable interest rates. When producers are able to store their crops and market them over an extended period, this helps to expand the domestic market as well as develop export markets.
In the past few years producers have become very involved in the marketing of their crops in order to improve their market return. They have learned that it does not pay to sell to the first buyer who comes along if they can hold their produce longer. Many producers' organizations have compared their returns to producers who participate in the Advance Payments for Crops Program with those who do not. It is noteworthy that the cost of the program is far less than the increased market return to producers.
Not surprisingly, participation in the program has increased considerably in the past few years. In the first year of the program, only eight producer organizations across the country participated. For the 1984-85 crop year, close to $190 million was guaranteed under the program through some 47 producer organizations. More than 18,000 producers benefited as a result of this program.
In addition to doubling the maximum size of this program, the proposed legislation includes several housekeeping amendments which could make the program more flexible. The first of these would clarify the definition of a buyer-broker and would specify who names them. This is necessary to allow producers greater flexibility in developing a marketing system that is best for them. Without that flexibility they tend to develop marketing systems that would make them eligible for payments under the Act.
The second housekeeping amendment would improve the means and fairness of collecting defaults and would permit the federal Government to pay associated legal costs. Under the Act producers' organizations are currently responsible for collecting bad debts or defaults. This means that all participat-
June 26, 1985

ing producers have to pay the expenses for those who default. The proposed legislation would allow the producers' organization to recover the collection costs from the producers who default. Failing that, their legal expenses would be paid for by the federal Government. Any legal expenses, however, would be offset by the savings on the interest charges on outstanding defaults. On this point I want to take a moment to reassure the House that the level of defaults is extremely small. In the seven years that the program has been in operation, the average total of the defaults is less than one tenth of 1 per cent of the total value of all payments guaranteed. The lending institutions consider their percentage of defaults in the agricultural sector as a good rate.
In addition, the proposed Bill includes a number of other housekeeping amendments that will help streamline the administrative process and allow for negotiation of lower interest rates. This should result in significant savings to the federal Government. All of the proposed amendments have been developed in concert with producer organizations and are generally supported by them. At a time when crop producers are under great stress from rising production costs and fluctuating market prices, the Advance Payments for Crops Program is more important than ever. By doubling the maximum advance payment level, the federal Government is providing the producers with a greater marketing tool and greater marketing opportunities. The Advance Payments for Crops Program has proved to be very worth-while and indeed a very necessary program. It is not as useful as it could be. It is a 1977 model which has not kept pace with 1985 market conditions.
It is for all of these reasons that I urge Members of the House to approve this Bill to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister mentioned the Class of '68. He was elected in 1972. As I recall, that was not particularly a good year for our side of the House. However, within 18 months we recovered sufficiently to continue on for another 12 years. I just thought I should draw that to the Minister's attention because I believe he has been here most of the time since then.
In a more serious vein, I wanted to indicate the support of the Official Opposition for the Advance Payments for Crops Act. This legislation was brought in back in 1977 when our Party was the Government. It is good Liberal legislation. Indeed, it was a plank in our election campaign platform last year that would have seen these payments doubled from $15,000 to $30,000, from $30,000 to $60,000 and from $45,000 to $90,000, depending on the number of producers involved. I have had representations on this legislation from the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board in Chatham and the Ontario Corn Producers Association. The have requested in the strongest possible terms that this legislation be passed this year so it would be available for crops in the coming year.
The legislation will provide assistance to non-Wheat Board commodities which are storable. It will help producers to
Advance Payments for Crops Act
stabilize their prices by not forcing them to put crops on the market during low price periods or to provide cash flow immediately after the crops have been taken off. It will as well avoid the forced sale of commodities, which often reduces the price. I believe it is important legislation. It has been on the books for a number of years, and these amendments will bring it up to date to meet the needs of 1985 and the future.
When the Minister was speaking he indicated there would be an opportunity in the future to increase the total amounts by way of an appropriation Bill rather than by bringing in a new Bill. When we go into committee stage I would be interested in learning the details of that and whether it would be done by a one dollar item, which I thought had been determined not to be acceptable to the Speaker. Perhaps the Minister will be able to explain that during committee stage of this Bill.
Over the past number of years this legislation has promoted development of crop storage facilities, because having the cash available and the interest of the federal Government is of great assistance in that regard. As I understand this legislation, it will increase the number of people to whom a producer can sell his crops. This will codify the existing situation. It is my understanding that in the past producers could only sell to a producer association or a co-operative but not to a neighbour. This legislation will provide for that.
Another important aspect has been that funds were often actually lent to associations such as the Ontario Corn Producers' Association and the Ontario Soybean Growers' Marketing Board. This legislation will assist those producers' associations to recover funds when the advance payment is not properly made. The interest costs under the existing program have been about $6 million a year. I understand that the Government will have to make provision for approximately $12 million a year under this program.
I would like to indicate the support of my Party for this legislation. It is useful legislation although it does not solve some of the major problems facing the agricultural industry in Canada today such as lower prices for many grain crops due to the American bonus plan for their grains. However, it allows producers to withhold from the market, during slump periods, those crops which are being adversely affected by that program in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I want to lend our support to the expeditious passage of this legislation in order that the benefits can be made available to the various producer groups which are affected.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise that Bill C-58, an Act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to give my Party's approval in principle for the proposal which the Government has brought forward, namely, to double the amount of interest-free cash advanced to producers of agricultural products outside of the Canadian Wheat Board area. This brings the rest of Canada into parity with producers who grow wheat, oats, barley, rye, and oil seeds in the western region. It permits them to make out an interest-free cash advance after harvest to a maximum of $30,000 per farm. It could be up to a maximum of $60,000 or $90,000 if there are two or three major operators on that farm.
As the Minister has pointed out, the losses through this program have been less than one-tenth of 1 per cent. It does provide ready cash for producers and enables them to withhold their products from the market immediately after harvest. They are able to ease their products on to the market over the course of the year.
This Bill does only good things from the point of view of agricultural marketing. It goes hand in glove with other programs of the last 15 or 20 years carried out by the Department with regard to storage of agricultural products. We approve this approach to agriculture and support the Bill heartily.

There is the B.C. Tree Fruits, dealing with apples, Bartlett pears and Anjou pears; B.C. Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, again with canola. In Manitoba we have CSP Foods, sunflower seeds; the Manitoba Vegetable Producers Marketing Board with potatoes, onions and rutabagas. Moving into Ontario we have Blue Water Storage, Norfolk Fruit Growers Association, primarily apples. We have the Ontario Soya-Bean Growers Marketing Board, the Ontario Apple Marketing Commission, the Ontario Burley Tobacco Growers Marketing Board, the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Board and the Ontario Corn Producers Association. I was interested in the representation which the Hon. Member for Algoma was reading on behalf of the Corn Growers of the province. Mr. Chairman, I believe under the existing legislation if there is a default by an individual producer in repaying the advance payment then the producer association or marketing board has to pay the legal fees and as well absorb the loss. I thought when the Minister was speaking he indicated not only would the federal Government provide the legal assistance to the marketing agency or Producers Association to recover those fees, but if the individual producer was in bankruptcy or ultimately was not able to repay the advance payment, then the federal Government would absorb it as well.
Can the Minister clarify if the arrangement is that all the legal fees and any defaults which occur will be absorbed by the federal Government? Can he advise, since we have been going through a rash of foreclosures and bankruptcies during 1984 and early 1985, just what the losses were during 1984 to producer associations and other groups under this legislation?

Mr. Chairman, I want to answer an earlier question put by the Hon. Member for Algoma. I think he
June 26, 1985

requested what percentage or how many dollars were utilized at the present time under the Act providing the $200 million ceiling. My information is that $183 million at the present time is utilized by the 47 producer organizations across the country.
I believe at the moment there is about $1 million in defaults.
I think it is about one-tenth of 1 per cent. I have it here in a chart, but 1 have so many charts it takes me some time to go through them. I believe the information I am supplying is accurate.
With respect to the changes in the Act dealing with the defaults, the current system places full responsibility for collecting defaults, including costs, on the producer organizations.
I think this is the observation which the Hon. Member made. This is very expensive for them and these costs are shared by all producers participating in the advance program by way of an administrative fee. The result is producers that repay their advances pay a higher fee to pay the expenses of those producers who default. These amendments will allow the producer organizations to recover the collection costs from the producer. If this cannot be done, the legal expenses will be paid by the federal Government and savings on interest charges on the outstanding defaults should offset any legal expenses that will have to be paid. I believe that should answer the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Algoma.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister will know that this particular Act applies to everything except wheat, oats, and barley sold under the Wheat Board, and there is a separate cash advance for those crops. There is a certain amount of crop utilization. On the Prairies where we grow some of the oil seeds, we use this Act, and we can still use the other cash advance for our wheat, oats and barley sold through the Canadian Wheat Board.
I am a little curious especially because this Act covers such a wide range of products. Can the Minister tell us what sort of information gathering system is used to make certain that an individual does not exceed the $30,000 maximum? While he is at it, can the Minister tell us whether it is possible for a farmer in my region, for instance, who might have borrowed $30,000 against his wheat, oats and barley through the Wheat Board, to take in addition a $30,000 cash advance on his potatoes? How do you monitor the differences to keep it down to $30,000 each as per the Act?

Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that one would be eligible to participate in one program or the other. This I believe is correct.
It is my understanding that the administration of both Acts is carried out by Agriculture Canada, and I would suspect by the same people within Agriculture Canada. Therefore, sufficient checks would be in place to ensure that the situation which the Hon. Member described should not happen, as far as I am concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the Minister is not saying that a producer could use $15,000 out of the wheat, oats and barley fund and an additional $15,000 for rapeseed and flaxseed, to get to his grand total of $30,000. I think some farmers are doing that now. However, I am curious to know what sorts of procedure is used for commodities other than Wheat Board grains.
I know from experience that the Wheat Board has to delay the issuance of cheques for the balance of advances for something like two weeks,to make certain that producers have not applied at three of four elevator companies for cash advances. It is possible for producers to take out advances at virtually any delivery point. It is possible for them to obtain half the advance for which they are eligible at three of four different points. The Wheat Board sits on the final issuance of cheques, monitors all applications and decides whether in fact a particular producer is eligible for the final amount.
Is a similar process in place for these advances? Can a participating organization or broker issue half the advance almost immediately, with the balance coming from a central organization through Agriculture Canada? What process is used?
I ask these questions of the Minister because there may be some producers watching this debate who have yet to set up agencies to provide for these advances. My next question will concern how they go about doing this, but I wanted to start with some of the procedures in place so that we would have that information on the record.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps we could talk about a few other minute details of the Bill. That would provide me with a moment or two in which to receive the detailed information requested by the Hon. Member, or at least have it sent to me. As I indicated in an earlier answer, if an individual wanted to participate in the two programs, it is possible, providing that he does not exceed the old 15 and the new 30, 60 and 90 levels.
I am assured that adequate administrative requirements are in place to ensure that duplication does not happen. I did not make a note of the Hon. Member's third question because my officials signalled me, indicating that that would not happen and that everything we need was in place for the proper administration of the program.
In the absence of any black and white information, the fact is that the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Program has been in effect for a good number of years. It has worked well. I cannot recall having encountered any serious difficulties with it. The Hon. Member is in a better position than I am to indicate what problems there have been with that piece of legislation, because he represents a part of the country which has received the benefits of that program for quite some time.
This Bill came along later, in 1977. To my knowledge there were only two problems. One was that levels were not high enough and the other was that participating agencies were concerned about some defaults. We are trying to deal with these two problems by increasing the maximum levels and by changing the way in which defaults are collected. We are

sharing some greater responsibility in that area by picking up the legal costs.
I should like to indicate some additional information. By reducing the potential liability to producer organizations from 5 per cent to 2 per cent, a better interest rate can be negotiated. This measure will reduce the average interest rate by up to one half or 1 per cent. No producer organization has exceeded the final default rate of 2 per cent over the last seen years of the operation of the program. As I indicated earlier, the average of defaults is less than one tenth of 1 per cent. That pretty well tells the story about advance payments, both prairie grain advance payments and the advance payments for crops with which we are dealing now.
It would appear to me that the necessary mechanisms, administrative personnel and procedures must be functioning reasonably well, or we would have heard about it by now. If the Hon. Member has some specific examples to raise, I would be happy to take notice of them, have my officials check into them and report back to him as soon as possible.

I wonder if the Minister could quickly go through the steps or rules for producers of commodities who are interested in negotiating an agreement for setting up an interest-free cash advance program. What steps would they have to go through? What volumes are required before a group or agency would be acceptable under the program?

I cannot give the Hon. Member the detailed requirements to which a marketing agency or marketing commission would be subjected. When the Bill was first brought forward in 1977, the Ontario Corn Council lobbied the previous Government unsuccessfully, to no avail. We took the position at that time that although the Ontario Corn Council was not a marketing board or marketing commission, it had the administrative powers, personnel and so on to take advantage of the advance payments for crops legislation in 1977. However, the Government of the day said no, rightly or wrongly. The Council has continued to lobby and of course has changed its organization. It has met the criteria of the Bill and has been participating in the adance payments legislation for the last two or three years, or about that period of time.
Existing marketing boards and commissions are in a position to take advantage of the legislation. A marketing board, commission or co-op would simply send the information to us. In fact, it could be sent to the Hon. Member, the Hon. Member could forward it to us, and we could take a look at the organizational structure to see whether or not it meets the criteria. If it meets the criteria, then of course it would participate in the program. If we look at the marketing organizations which have participated, they run from co-ops to marketing agencies, commissions and wheat pools. The list goes on and on.
If there is a marketing group or organization-probably not an organization, I think that terminology is a little too loose- we will have a look at it. Generally they have to be legally
incorporated and included in the marketing of a crop. They must be able to administer the program and must represent a significant portion of the production in the area. Again, we would need to have evidence that they were legally incorporated, included in the marketing of a crop, able to administer the program and represent a significant portion of the production in that area.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Minister can give us an approximation of how many such groups have been established since 1977, to which cash advances are now in effect.

Mr. Chairman, I think I touched that in my notes. I indicated that the program had grown quite rapidly over the years since 1977. I believe I indicated that there was a very small number of co-ops and marketing agencies that participated in the program in the first year and, I believe, I indicated that last year we had 47 organizations in the program across the country. As you will know, Mr. Speaker, from having read the Bill and being thoroughly acquainted with it, this Bill is permissive legislation which sets out an umbrella under which producers, the provincial Governments and the federal Government can go together to strike a tripartite agreement to stabilize farm prices.
One thing that we heard most often from provinces across the country was that they were concerned about going into these agreements without having some feeling of acceptance or right to raise the possibility of variations in production costs from one end of the country to the other. They felt that there should be some way that would enable them to bring to the discussions the question of the particular costs that they have that are particular to their region, to put those on the table and negotiate the kind of system that is needed for a tripartite system across the country.
Because this is a government Bill, and the motivation is here and the expenditure plans that limit what a private member or an opposition Member can do, this is one of the few places where it is possible to bring the question of regional costs into the discussions. It would be under the section of the activities of the board that was established to look at the costing formula, either for those products that come under the program under the old Agricultural Stabilization Act or products which would come under by tripartite agreements between the various producer groups in the country, some or all of the provinces and the federal Government. This is one of the few spots where it is possible to mention the fact that regional costs can be a concern.
This would put a discussion of these various costs onto the table and permit the various groups to discuss costs that are unique to their parts of the country. For instance, there are high energy costs paid by Prince Edward Island farmers who produce hogs or dairy products. These farmers are required to spend a great deal of money on electricity to run the machinery and sometimes even to provide additional heat.
Representatives from other regions of the country mentioned that feed costs were relatively higher in their regions than in other parts of the country, and they said that they would like to be able to discuss this in the negotiations that take place prior to agreeing to a tripartite system. In fact, they mentioned that they would even like to be able to permit some slight variation with agreement from all of the participating groups as part of the final agreement.
In committee, we heard from representatives of the Province of British Columbia, a province which has had the most experience with an income stabilization program. Those representatives told us that when that program began, there was some allowance for regional differences in costs from one valley to another for the various payout levels in the production of tomatoes and other such crops. However, the representatives went on to point out that as time went on, it became obvious even to the producers that some of these cost disadvantages were offset by advantages in other portions of production
Agricultural Stabilization Act
costs and that eventually regional cost variations were seen to be unnecessary. Therefore, the producers themselves took regional cost variations out of the program.
It is my contention that once producers can see all of the various cost items that producers from their areas and other areas have to face, they will see that there is a real reason for their particular product being produced in their particular corner of the country. There is no doubt that hogs will continue to be produced in Prince Edward Island, Quebec and right across to British Columbia whether or not there is a tripartite stabilization program. While Quebec may have some disadvantages in the area of feed costs, it has an advantage over other parts of the country in labour costs, in the technical programs that are in place and because of the fact that its production units are somewhat superior to those in other parts of the country. That would balance off against the relatively lower cost of grain in Saskatchewan where the production units may not as a general rule be quite up to the competitive standards of those in Quebec.
I maintain that it all evens out. What I am fearful of in permitting this Bill to go through the way it is written without some recognition of regional cost variations is that we will leave the impression on those groups that think they have a particular cost disadvantage that there is no point in coming forward to the bargaining table to participate in the process. The idea behind this particular amendment is to make the umbrella slightly larger so that more producer groups from more provinces will feel comfortable under that umbrella and will begin the discussions preliminary to the establishment of a tripartite program. I think that this amendment sends the message that all producer groups from all across Canada are welcome under that umbrella and that their particular viewpoints and problems will be discussed fully. It will not leave them with the impression that we are excluding some groups while accepting others. That is why I have moved this amendment to the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. This is an important Bill. It may be that it is only enabling legislation but once it is in place, the federal Government has a commitment to support these producer groups. It is very unclear whether any of the producer groups in those four provinces will support the legislation as it was passed in the committee, so we are going to have to see whether they will support the legislation and what the prospects are for other groups such as the Quebec hog producers and the Maritime producers. At the same time, it does not seem to have

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party. I may say that the Hon. Member's intentions are entirely laudable and that consideration of regional costs is certainly one objective we can all support.
Mr. Speaker, in committee, and especially at the committee meeting last Thursday, Members had a chance to ask some very serious questions about the Government's intentions, and especially about the consultation process initiated by the Government. We were told by Quebec producers that the legislation was tabled without prior consultation and that there had been no formal consultation with the President of the Union des producteurs agricoles.
We also heard that Progressive Conservative Members had tried to persuade the Minister to change his mind about this Bill and delay consideration until comprehensive consultation had taken place, but unfortunately, the Minister refused to consider these requests.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the House provides an opportunity to discuss regional differences in Canada, and I know the minister is one of the true believers in the community of communities theory. During the few years when the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was Leader of the Party and Prime Minister, the Minister supported his community of communities theory. However, it seems the Minister has a very short memory, because now he would like to stabilize poverty, as it were, by providing for uniformity over and above regional differences. However, considering how well the Minister knows the country and its regional differences, I am confident that he will find this amendment acceptable. In committee, the Minister spent some time on this issue, and I hope that today, he will be able to give us a definitive answer and vote in favour of the amendment. In fact, this amendment gives us a chance to reopen the whole debate on the constitutional responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments for agriculture. In this respect, the Bill before the House and even the amendments presented by the Minister in committee are not likely to be satisfactory to the provincial parties.
The Minister is well aware that his Quebec counterpart cannot accept the provisions of this Bill. He knows perfectly well that Quebec producers object to the prerequisites imposed by this legislation. Nevertheless, he insists on using his party's overwhelming majority and the silence of Quebec Conservative Members to impose his vision of uniformity across the country. Mr. Speaker, I still think that the Minister has a chance, today
Agricultural Stabilization Act
at the report stage and in the next few days at third reading, to show that he has really been listening to his colleagues from Quebec, instead of hoisting their arms and asking them to keep quiet, and that he has been listening to the caucus and as a result will have a far more satisfactory solution to show for it.
Mr. Speaker, we heard from representatives of the UPA, the Federation of Pork Producers, the Federation of Lamb Producers, and people in the cattle industry, and from their testimony before the committee, it was clear they wanted us to recognize two principles.
First, they said they were convinced that it would be better for Canadian agriculture to have income stabilization than price stabilization. Of course there is a very basic difference of opinion on this principle. But they also said, in referring to the provinces that within their respective jurisdictions had decided to implement specific agricultural policies to protect their farmers that they were anxious to see these provinces continue within the framework of the national system, to administer the programs they initiated and were supporting with their tax revenues.
Mr. Speaker, this debate has been going on for a long time, and I am referring to the right of the provinces to make decisions with respect to agriculture policy. The Minister knows perfectly well that for instance, in the case of Quebec, its policy of food self-sufficiency may well be jeopardized by the passage of this Bill. The Minister realizes this and I know his Quebec counterpart has said, and I quote: I am trying to show that the approach you have opted for with respect to red meat stabilization is dangerous and discriminatory.
He is saying: You take a discriminatory approach when, on one hand you refuse to give pork producers the money owed to them or to acknowledge the right of the provinces to manage their own stabilization programs-for fear that the Americans might retaliate-and, on the other hand you give hundreds of millions of dollars to western grain producers. Besides your attitude might very well jeopardize the interests of pork producers and processors in their current conflict with the American Government. The provincial Minister goes on to say: The Canadian Pork Council and the Canadian Meat Council are spending tens of thousands of dollars to hire lawyers to defend them. Those lawyers are trying to prove to the American Government that funds received under stabilization programs must not be considered as prejudicial grants since they are in fact permanent insurance measures partially financed by the farming community and whose benefits must be spread over a long period of time, in keeping with actuarial principles. The Minister is saying: Through your statements you demolish the thesis they defend, you condemn Canadian pork producers even before American and international courts of law have made a judgment. I am drawing inspiration from a document drafted by the Quebec Government. He goes on to say: On behalf of Quebec pork producers we are entitled to expect more from the Canadian Minister of Agriculture whose re-

June 26, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
sponsibility is to uphold the interests of Canadian agricultural producers no matter the sector where they try to earn a living or the province where they live. You must stop taking advantage of the current predicament of pork producers to rush this Bill through. That is the key word, and that is what we are witnessing, Mr. Speaker. They are trying to push this measure right through, but I am sure they will be up against stiff opposition in the next few hours and days because we are determined, Mr. Speaker, to use all our parliamentary rights to bring the Minister to his senses or at least convince him to go back to the consultation process.
The Minister knows as well as I and all other Members of the House do that this Bill is unacceptable to the producers of a province and to many others. The list is getting longer every day and we are trying to make him understand that he is being overly hasty. He is acting today against the best judgment of everybody. He may be able to get his own colleagues to stand still for this, but he will not be able to prevent the producers from speaking up. Instead of trying to put them before a fait accompli the Minister should make sure that the producers have their say before he imposes this measure.
After lengthy discussions, Mr. Speaker, the Minister finally introduced an amendment in committee, but I voted against it because it did not satisfy anyone. The Minister came up with an amendment which apparently was quite satisfactory to Department of Justice officials, but they were practically the only ones to feel that way. I have yet to hear from one producer or one organization that would be prepared to support the amendment. I certainly hope the Minister will be able to produce a series of supporting telegrams he received in the last few hours. If the Minister can convince me that this amendment is acceptable to the farmers I represent, I would be prepared to reconsider my position because I think my duty here is to speak for the producers who came to see me and urged me to prevent this Bill from being pushed through. We have nothing against the principle of stabilization, but the Minister will have to show more flexibility if he seeks to rally the various interests. The Minister did not listen to his colleagues and I am afraid he will not listen to Opposition Members either, but he will learn his lesson in the field, Mr. Speaker. If the Minister cannot be more flexible with us, I would ask him to be flexible and almost courageous with his American friends because it does look as though the Government wants to use the pork crisis as an excuse to push this Bill through and make us believe that it has to be the ultimate solution. But, Mr. Speaker, no one in the farming sector believes that this is the answer to everything. The Minister may say that, at the time, the Liberal Government had introduced a similar bill, but that could be one of the reasons why there are now fewer of us on this side. The Minister should learn from what happened after the last elections. He should remember the promises of his colleagues who said that
this measure would be amended. Where are those amendments?
The Minister tried to pass off a facsimile of what his predecessor had introduced. At the time, we of the Quebec caucus had officially objected to this legislation because we believed that it was unfair and not quite finalized because there had not been enough consultation and flexibility.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the Minister seems to believe he is the only one with the answer. He says that he alone holds the truth: Pass this Bill and we shall see later!
Mr. Speaker, it is not that I do not trust the Minister, because I know that he is an honest man and has a very good reputation, but I am not convinced that I want to give him a free hand. If we pass this Bill in haste and give a free hand to the Minister, we shall jeopardize the existence of provincial programs established under the jurisdiction of the provinces as defined by the Canadian Constitution. Mr. Speaker, as you know, you can be for the Constitution as you can be for virtue and motherhood. In this optic-

What is more, it does not contain the least requirement for the partners to consider the production cost variations from one

region to the next. As far as pork is concerned, for instance, higher prices in Toronto and lower production costs in the Prairies will contribute to set up a national chart which will not take into account the actual situation in Quebec and, as a result, the compensations under the proposed federal system will be reduced to a minimum.
However, Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by my colleague of the New Democratic Party deals specifically with the need to take into account clearly and precisely the estimated production costs of farm products in a given region, and such an amendment is essential. If we want to have a fair program which will satisfy all producers in all regions of the country, the real costs in each region must be taken into account. I am surprised that the Government does not accept this amendment. I believe that it is essential if we really want to have a fair program.
During the few minutes left to me, I would like to come back to the comments of the Hon. Member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Gerin), who criticized my colleague for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) for having referred to a working paper prepared by the Quebec Department of Agriculture. It is a fact that what my colleague from Shefford quoted was a working paper and not a letter duly signed and sent by the Minister to his federal counterpart, but this working paper, which has been made public, is quite revealing, and I would like to quote just a few words from it to show to what extent this so-called spirit of co-operation between the Governments of Canada and Quebec seems to have dissolved, at least as far as agriculture is concerned. The Quebec Minister of Agriculture had no need to send a letter to state publicly that, in his opinion, the federal Government and especially the Minister of Agriculture have not done a good job in the interests of Quebec pork producers, that he felt the Government of Canada could never solve the problem our hog producers are faced with because this Conservative administration seems unduly concerned about antagonizing the Reagan administration. Ever since it assumed power, this Conservative Government has repeatedly emphasized the need to develop and maintain good and friendly relations with the American President. That is fine and dandy, provided that they benefit Canadians in the long run. A good place to start could have been in respect of Quebec hog producers who have been wronged and completely deceived during the last election campaign by Conservative candidates with a promise of additional cheques. They are still waiting for these cheques from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) who made this solemn promise to Quebec hog producers, and now the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) would like the House to rubber-stamp Bill C-25 with a total disregard for the objections raised by Quebec farm producers and their own interests.
The document which my colleague the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) referred to needs no comments. For instance: "In order to push through Bill C-25, the Government is bent on creating the impression that the continuation of provincial programs could mean a complete disaster for producers, and that failure to adopt this Bill now before the Summer recess could start a bloody war between the provinces". If we continue with our provincial programs-I conclude my remarks with this, Mr. Speaker-the next move the United States could make could be higher taxes, increased import quotas or even an embargo. That borders on blackmail, and I ask the Minister of Agriculture to show his good faith by delaying the adoption of this Bill in order to consult all interested parties. And if the Conservative Government wants to remain on friendly terms with the current Quebec Government, he should ask the Quebec Minister of Agriculture to appear before our committee and say what he really thinks of Bill C-25. Until then, I think that Quebec producers will suffer as a result of this Bill which will cause them irreparable damage.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about Bill C-25. I have a great deal of concern about the Bill and I must say that I will not be able to support it simply because regional costs are not taken into consideration.
I have with me a telegram that was sent to me by the Minister of Agriculture in the Province of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Prowse Chappell. The subject of the telegram is the red meat stabilization Bill, Bill C-25. He indicates in the telegram that on June 6, 1985, his Department made a presentation to the Standing Committee on Agriculture regarding the Bill.
He stressed two points at that time of very vital interest to the Province of Prince Edward Island. First, potatoes which is the number one commodity in agriculture production in Prince Edward Island, should be included in the list of named commodities, thereby qualifying our most important commodity for mandatory support under the Stabilization Act.
The importance of potatoes to the Province of Prince Edward Island and the Province of New Brunswick, he goes on to say, would be compared to grains in western Canada, for which we all know separate legislation is in place under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. His second recommendation is that Bill C-25 be amended to permit the recognition of legitimate regional costs in national plans. Regional costs do not exist, and failure to address them on an equitable basis will frustrate-this is what the Minister is saying to me in a telegram-our common objectives, our harmonizing support programs. By way of amendment, P.E.I. has suggested the deletion of Section 8.10.1(3) and the addition of the following Section 8.10.14(A): agreement must specify and take into account regional production costs. That is signed by the Hon. P. Chappell, Minister of Agriculture, province of Prince Edward Island.

He is not a Liberal.
June 26, 1985

He is not a Liberal, no. But I want to get back to the regional costs. If you have a national program that does not take into consideration-and I hope the Minister is listening very carefully to this-
I am always listening.

-the difference in cost of production of hogs, beef, whatever, but certainly hogs in the Province of Prince Edward Island, what use is it? In my province, Prince Edward Island, it costs probably $15 to $20 more to produce a hog than in the Province of Alberta. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) shaking his head.
I am not agreeing with you. I am listening.
He says he is not agreeing with me but he is listening. If the Minister is not agreeing with me, then he is not agreeing with the Minister of Agriculture in the Province of P.E.I. either.

Where is this so-called consultation which this Government has gone on about for so many months and the great harmony between the provinces and the federal Government? The Minister has to admit in this Chamber today that consultation is a one-way process as far as this Government is concerned.
Tory arrogance.
It is a one-way process.
No.

You are not listening to the Minister of Agriculture for the Province of Prince Edward Island. Therefore, the Minister of Agriculture is not listening to the farmers of P.E.I. or Atlantic Canada.
Let me give an indication of the excessive costs that we have to bear as farmers in Prince Edward Island. First, we have the extreme high cost of electricity. Hon. Members know very well one has to take into consideration electricity costs, transportation costs and feed grains. When one adds up those costs, my province finds it is impossible to compete with other parts of the country when it comes to hogs.
My province and the Government of Prince Edward Island, which is of a blue stripe, has tried to promote the agricultural industry to the point where I think it is crazy to go ahead with the kind of kill and chill plant it is considering. I think most farmers in my province will agree that it is too grandiose for the situation as it is today in Prince Edward Island. It is a legitimate Government and I might say the actions that have been carried on in the last while will not allow it to be the Government for very much longer.
Having said that, it is the Government, the legitimate Government of P.E.I. I am amazed, I am astounded, that the Minister of Agriculture is not listening to the Minister of Agriculture for the Province of P.E.I. Why would that
Agricultural Stabilization Act
happen? I can tell the Minister something else. Here is a telegram that I have received from Mr. Keith Russell, Executive Secretary, Maritime Farmers Council. It is dated June 24. It reads:
Please be reminded that the National Red Meat Stabilization Plan will need to reflect regional variations in production costs in order to be useful to Maritime livestock producers.
I guess that says it all. If you were a hog farmer or a beef farmer in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, then I think you would be very reluctant to get into a program that had as an average cost something far above the cost of your production. Too long have farmers in Canada been producing crops and selling them at below the cost of production.
That is right.

This stabilization program which the Minister is talking about in Bill C-25 does nothing to alleviate that situation. In fact, as my hon. friend just mentioned, it stabilized poverty for those people in those areas. I am amazed my good friend, the Minister of Agriculture, would bring in a Bill at this time that would not reflect the realities of this great country of ours. There are areas where you can produce goods, farm produce at one price and there are areas where that costs more. It is unfortunate that we happen to live in an area in Atlantic Canada that is a little far removed from the mainstream of the population. We are geographically dislocated, if you will, from the market.
What about B.C.?

Yes, B.C. At least B.C. stretches a little north and south, but B.C. as well. I agree with the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King). I know the great apples his agricultural community produce in B.C. Certainly I do not see anything in this Bill that would do anything for his apple crop.
Nothing.
That is not right.

I cannot understand my friend. He says it is not right. I hope he will stand in his place and tell me why it is not right because I do not see anything in this Bill that says you are going to get one iota from Bill C-25.
The Minister has brought in a Bill to say that he has done something for the agricultural community of the country. I am afraid it is nothing but a sham. He is not taking into account regional costs and not taking into consideration potatoes, and he is eliminating a number of other situations when it comes to feed grains coming east. The economic statement in November and the Budget sort of alluded to the fact that some of these subsidies may well be dropped. Some of the great benefits that we enjoyed over the last number of years were beginning to erode. Unless the Minister starts to take a fresh view of this, then I think he should scrap this Bill right here today as far as I am concerned and as far as P.E.I. is concerned. He should

speechtext: That is nonsense, absolutely flap-doodle.

Mr. Speaker, agriculture has changed. It has changed on a world-wide basis and on a national basis, but particularly on a national basis. I am sure that my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island is quite aware that there have been pleadings in this Chamber and in committee meetings in the last 15 years that the Government should address the price stabilization programs which it was authorized to operate. The Government of the day refused to do it, and it continued to do that on a declining basis.
Historically, as long as there was meaningful price stabilization action on the part of the federal Government, massive bankruptcies were avoided in the farm sector. Rarely, if ever, did it contribute to profit, but it served as a "stop loss" operation. Those commodities which required price stabilization in a given year may have experienced a 1 per cent or 2 per cent reduction and may have been compelled, by virtue of the fact that there was no profit, to reduce their production. As a result of the nature of that program and without massive hardship, production of agricultural products in Canada was controlled to meet market demands. For most people agriculture was never a supply of wealth, but it supplied an average income for people who persisted in that sphere. Few became wealthy and, historically, few went broke.
However, when the concept of price stabilization was abandoned, we got into difficulty because the provinces of Canada entered the field. When they became involved in the maintenance of the agricultural industry province by province, they were not satisfied with that. Instead, they not only tried to maintain the production of individual commodities, but tried to expand them. That is understandable. Thus we have within this nation a quarrel among the provinces as to who will produce what and how much.
This is the first piece of legislation which has given Agriculture Canada, provincial Ministers of Agriculture and farmers an opportunity to sit around a table and judge for themselves what is in the best interests of various commodities in the long term and how they can find the stable position of production with assured income so that they can continue to farm. If we continue in the interprovincial battle, there is no question that agriculture would be totally dislocated, that geography, climate and soil capability would be ignored, that we would be producing products in some parts of Canada which were never intended to be produced there by nature, and that man would spend a fortune in an effort to produce what nature did not plan. That is with what we are faced.
The first real breakdown in the refusal of the Liberal Party as a Government to come to the aid of agriculture was when the cattle industry asked for a price stabilization program. The initial estimated cost of that program, just as a break even
deal, was $300 million. It was rejected out of hand by the Liberal Government of that day. Since that point in time, the red meat industry has been in difficulty and provinces have been competing with one another, using farmers as their tools.
I say to the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) that basically the requests of Atlantic Ministers of Agriculture have been recognized. There is now judgmental opportunity in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to consider provincial differences. However, what is more important is the piece of legislation which is in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture. It can properly start negotiations with the producers and the Ministers of Agriculture of all provinces, regardless of their political stripe. The consultative process which this puts in place gives some opportunity for avoiding war between the provinces and disparate conditions for individual farmers and their individual products.
For instance, I refer to the case of apples. The trade picture is not as it was. Trade agreements have been made which allow subsidized products to come into Canada to the detriment of the farming community. Whether it be apples or apple processed products, whether it be red meat, whether it be grapes, wine and wine products, they are coming into Canada on a free access basis, without constraint, as a result of utterly and totally ridiculous international trade agreements which were made against the advice of organized agriculture in Canada for the last 25 years. The policy of the Government of Canada has been: Let us trade off agriculture trading opportunities and let us build the manufacturing industry of Canada. As a result, the Canadian market has been glutted with imported food and we have a $10 billion to $15 billion trade deficit in manufactured products. We lost at both ends of the scale.
The international production figure has changed. No statistic was presented to the committee, as it considered this Bill, which emphasized that any more than the following facts. Fifteen years ago Canada was trading apples and exporting as many as it was receiving. Perhaps in most years it exported more than it imported. Today we are importing many more than we are exporting because of bad trade agreements and because of increased production which is subsidized in such places as the Pacific Rim by the Governments of those areas which no longer need our apples.
The potato industry finds itself in the same position. It is constrained by artificial barriers to trade, as the Hon. Member for Egmont well knows. We find ourselves, commodity by commodity, in a position which is uncomfortable and one which can only be addressed by consultation. We cannot continue any longer without joining forces in Canada on a non-competitive basis, with an urge for a province to own a product and its production.
I have particular fear for Atlantic Canada because it does not have the money to compete with the other provinces. Agriculture will suffer more than it can stand under those circumstances. I believe that the Ministers of Agriculture of Atlantic Canada are not totally satisfied, nor are they totally satisfied in Alberta or Ontario. This piece of legislation does not particularly fit the plan or wish of provinces, but it sets up

a framework under which they can all sit around the table to discuss it, something which could never be accomplished before.
I can speak for the Province of New Brunswick and its hog industry because I have consulted with them. The magnitude of the changes to this Act versus the way in which it was introduced does not totally please them. It does not totally please the Hon. Prowse Chappell or the Hon. Malcolm MacLeod. However, it is a compromise with which they can live and which will serve Canadian agriculture better than any other solution which I have heard proposed in my lifetime in this House.
