Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for your admirable introduction.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the amendment presented by the Member of the New Democratic Party and perhaps take advantage of this opportunity to speak to the Bill in a more general way.
Mr. Speaker, the riding I represent in Ontario is in a region that differs somewhat from other regions across the country, and I am sure that every Member in this House feels the same about his riding or region, which I think is quite normal and quite human.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to elaborate on this issue of regional differences. As you know yourself, Mr. Speaker, since you represent a riding about 100 miles from my own, which is pretty close, the situation in agriculture in Eastern Ontario is not only rather different from the rest of the country but also differs from the rest of the province, and perhaps I should explain. For instance, hog producers in my riding sell their products on the Quebec market, and their production costs are similar to those of Quebec producers. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Quebec is across the fence, as it were, from my riding, since my riding is on the Quebec border, so that producers in the region I represent are quite a distance from Southwestern Ontario, for instance, which grows most of the feed grains for hogs and where feed prices are much lower than in my riding and in Quebec. However, the region I represent does not benefit from the various provincial programs existing in Quebec, which is quite normal because we are in Ontario. So we see the people in my riding, with a market, prices production costs similar to those in Quebec, being offered the very marginal profits available in the province of Ontario. This means that a region like mine can be at a great disadvantage if regional differences in production costs are not considered. In my view, when we are talking about regional differences in production costs-and I do not mean provincial, although in this context, regional is often used to
Agricultural Stabilization Act
mean provincial-if the region I represent is not accommodated in some particular way within the Province of Ontario, we will again find ourselves at a definite disadvantage, similar to the situation in the Gaspe as compared with the rest of Quebec. So this is a phenomenon we find in certain regions in the outer reaches, as it were, of certain provinces. That is why there must be a mechanism to allow for differences in production costs, as I said earlier, but this mechanism does not necessarily have to apply strictly throughout a particular province. I think there is a case for designating certain regions within provinces, in order to allow for certain situations as is already being done through a number of joint programs on the Ontario side, for instance, where we have the Eastern Ontario Development Corporation which helps farmers make drainage improvements priced at a rate that differs from the going rate in Southeastern Ontario because there are special reasons for doing so. They are providing certain benefits for this disadvantaged region, and my point is that it has created a precedent for doing the same thing in other areas in agriculture and also in other sectors in industry, for instance. What we should do, as I mentioned to the Minister in committee and to his Parliamentary Secretary who is here in the House today, is to accommodate these regions in some way so that producers are not at a disadvantage. One of the problems, and the Minister is probably aware of this, is that it is very difficult to find out what advantages do exist in certain regions, although it may be easy in some cases.

For instance, if we are discussing top loading programs, it is fairly easy to identify where they exist and where they do not. On the other hand, if some regions offer other programs such as bottom loading and side loading programs and so forth, they are sometimes quite a bit harder to identify. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why such programs have not been as open to countervailing as others and have not been seen as having so many advantages or disadvantages.
I will give you an instance, Mr. Speaker. In the Province of Ontario, rural hydro rates are roughly 20 per cent to 25 per cent higher than urban rates. That is not the case in every Canadian province. If in a province the rural rates and the urban rates for electricity are the same, some people will argue that it costs more to service a rural area. Is that rural area then deemed to have received a subsidy on its electricity, for instance? I would argue not. I would argue that right now farmers of Ontario, through past provincial Conservative Governments, have suffered immensely because of this hydro policy. I see that the Minister is agreeing that the rural hydro rates in Ontario should be equal to the urban rates. I am glad to see that he is agreeing with that. I am sure that the new Liberal Government in Ontario will take note of that approval and hopefully will correct the shortcomings of the previous Tory Government very shortly.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) will recognize in the way that I have explained it, I hope, that it is difficult to determine which areas receive other advantages. It is difficult

June 26, 1985
Agricultural Stabilization Act
in some cases to determine the cost of production because not every province at the present time uses the same formula to determine it. It is a difficult proposition and everyone recognizes that. I am sure the Minister does. Nevertheless, the farmers that I represent in the existing situation, where they are losing money every day that they operate, in comparison with others in other parts of Ontario, need to have a mechanism by which their regional differences are accommodated.
One member on the Standing Committee of Agriculture said that is fine. What if somebody wants to start a pork production industry in a totally remote area? Are we then going to accommodate with special subsidies that very remote area which has not been producing before? I recognize that that could potentially be a problem.
However, the area that I represent has been producing pork for some time. Therefore, the problem is not that the area is remote, or new in terms of having that production. The Minister will recognize that the problem is that when times were good our farmers were making less money than others, but they were still making a profit. Now that times are more difficult, other farmers in certain areas are either making just a little bit of money or losing just a little bit and ours, with the disadvantage that is there, are losing even more. That is what puts the farmers of the area that I represent at a disadvantage, and that must be recognized and corrected in any legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-25, and of course on the amendment presented by the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party.
Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may-and I think I should, at this stage-digress somewhat and try to put this debate into context. I think we should recall that a month from now, we will be celebrating the first anniversary of the start of the election campaign. At the time, Hon. Members opposite were travelling around the rural ridings, meeting farmers and promising them security, stability and a good future in agriculture.
Admittedly such a commitment may at first have appeared quite challenging and quite attractive. I can therefore understand why a good many agricultural ridings voted for the Conservative candidates, sincerely believing as they did that a new Government would advocate measures and programs designed to stabilize and make more secure such a vital and strategic sector of the Quebec economy as agriculture. That same Government kept repeating during the last few weeks before the election: We are firmly committed to consult all interested parties, we are firmly committed to co-operate with all provincial Governments. Those were very challenging commitments, a sort of preview of what the very important agricultural sector might become.
Shortly after the election the Government introduced Bill C-25. In my opinion, the amendment of our colleague has to do with one of the most important aspects of this Bill. Before the committee and the commission there was a lot of talk about the major obstacles and barriers with respect to diversity, disparities and the fact that the same kind of production cost a lot more in the east than in the west. That is indeed one of the aspects of this Bill which has been the subject of many comments and strong opposition. As to the Minister, he tried to use a problem which is also very important to Quebec, namely the current instability of pork production.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the Minister of Agriculture who I should think is a very reliable spokesman for Quebec's agricultural community. Referring to the attitude of the Government concerning the pork issue, he said that the federal Minister had used this threat-obviously the American approach to this matter-had used this threat to sell a controversial red meat stabilization Bill instead of defending the interests of pork producers. He-still referring to our Minister of Agriculture-used the American threat to defend his own Bill. So the Minister concluded that there is a conflict of interests.
Not long before he said that, Mr. Speaker, the same Minister of Agriculture of Quebec had stated-and this can be readily understood-that the Government had been less enthusiastic in defending the interests of Quebec pork producers faced with the American surtax.
Quebec Agriculture Minister Garon pointed out that this case had been very badly defended by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and by the Minister of Agriculture. Naturally this is a current problem which is of major importance to the Quebec producers, so the Minister took that as an example to try to make us believe that with a stabilization measure such as Bill C-25 there would be no more problems with the American administration. Indeed the same Minister said in committee that he had consulted the Americans and discussed with them to try to anticipate what might be their reaction should Bill C-25 be adopted. I find it amazing and quite unacceptable that the Minister of Agriculture of Canada would rather listen to our friends to the south, the Americans, instead of taking the advice of every single APU farmer, an organization which happens to be the main spokesman under these circumstances. The Minister of Agriculture is trying to push through a Bill which is clearly and totally unfair to the Quebec agricultural community, unfair for a number of reasons.
First, everyone is aware of the fact that Quebec has stabilization programs which have been developed, put together, amended and improved throughout the years, to such an extent that Quebec ahas had in recent years good and even excellent stabilization programs which have provided some stability and security to the producers who make use of them.
June 26, 1985

Bill C-25 expressly and clearly states that, to join the program, it is absolutely essential to forget or to put aside the provincial program. This is completely unacceptable. It seems to me that this Bill could have provided something really interesting, positive and with great potential. If the Government had introduced substantially the same measure while allowing the provinces to keep their own stabilization programs, if the measure had explained how production costs would be taken into account, if, as my colleague from the New Democratic Party would like, some allowance had been made for the diversity which typifies Canada, I believe that we would have had a very acceptable Bill, for the greatest good of agriculture. However, the Minister seems adamant in wanting to have this Bill passed when we know that it constitutes an absolutely fundamental obstacle to agricultural choices in Quebec for many production sectors, such as pork, and to accept and endorse or support this Bill would be an incredible affront to the Quebec farming community. Mr. Speaker, agriculture comes under federal jurisdiction, but no one would dare to suggest that it is exclusively so. The provincial Government shares jurisdiction in this area, and in my opinion, if we want to respect this sharing of jurisdiction, we must recognize the possibility of also having provincial stabilization programs.
Obviously, because of its climate, of its differences as far as certain productions are concerned, Quebec must face substantially higher costs than our Western friends, and I believe that to give a uniform price or to contemplate or hope for uniformity is to discriminate clearly against our producers.
Mr. Speaker, the Quebec producers, of whom many came to meet us and who, I know, have met many of our friends opposite, strongly object to this Bill because it jeopardizes many sectors of the agricultural industry in Quebec. At a time when we need jobs and security so badly, when we need this economic sector to be the most prosperous in the world, we have to support Quebec producers in their requests that they be entitled to a minimum. Everyone recognizes that the purpose of this Bill is not to stabilize income, but rather to stabilize prices, and in this regard, as Canadians, we have naturally a duty to allow uniformity, but only if we take into account individual characteristics which are extremely numerous in the agricultural industry. If the Government was honest and sincere when expounding its desire to operate in an atmosphere of openness, communication and consultation, it can certainly not ignore the consensus surrounding this Bill in Quebec and must take into account what all the members of the farming community want, namely adjustments which will allow them to keep their own stabilization programs, and this for the greatest good of agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-25. Like my colleagues who spoke previously, I must say that I have some grave reservations about the content and, indeed, some of the omissions
Agricultural Stabilization Act
from Bill C-25. I don't like to use the word "errors" but certainly there are some omissions.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is aware of what the Government of Prince Edward Island has said about the inclusion of potatoes in Clause 1(1 )(a). I hope that the Minister will act on his comments forthwith. The Government of Prince Edward Island also went on to talk abouit other sections in the Bill which we find very disturbing, particularly as they affect those farmers who reside and operate in Atlantic Canada.
I am also in receipt of a telegram from the Maritime Farmers Council which expresses grave concern about the lack of content in Bill C-25. In addition, the Federation of Agriculture in Nova Scotia has expressed some deep concerns which I believe are justified. It believes it is imperative, on behalf of the pork producers in Nova Scotia, that Hon. Members oppose the Bill in its present form because it does not allow for regional cost of production or the continuation of its provincial hog stabilization program.
I know the Minister has attempted to embark on a consultative process and that has gone on all across the country with various interest groups. I want to convey to the Minister with sincerity and frankness that the farmers in the Maritime provinces are particularly concerned. There is not very much Clause 8, Section 10.1(3), to protect the livelihood of those farmers in the Maritimes. I think that is an omission. If it is an error, the Minister has the opportunity to right this wrong, but I believe it is an omission which has to be corrected.
It is my belief that the evidence which was given before the Standing Committee on Agriculture by the Maritime Farmers Council clearly indicates it would be supportive of the Bill, but it has a number of caveats which I believe are legitimate. I don't believe it is being partisan. I think it is speaking with the united voice of farmers in the Maritime provinces. I believe Hon. Members of Parliament on all sides of the House should concede to its requests.
The Council has said it is prepared to participate in such a program as outlined in Bill C-25 provided that the program adequately reflects the variation in the cost of production among the various regions of Canada so that its net benefits will be equalized among livestock producers all across the country. That is pretty fair and reasonable. That is something which emanates from the Charter and the new Constitution when we talk about equal opportunity. I know Hon. Members opposite may laugh at that, but it is a pretty serious issue to the Maritime farmers.
I want to say to the Minister that the major factor in calculating the cost of production in the livestock enterprise is the cost of feed. In the Maritime provinces this is particularly evident in the cost of production of pork because hogs are fed on grains and protein concentrates. The Maritimes only produces 42 per cent of our feed grain requirements and less than 5 per cent of our vegetable protein concentrates. The rest is imported from western and central Canada.

The Minister has a proposal before him which is supported by the Maritime Farmers Council and all of its organizations. It is supported by the provincial Governments of those provinces. It has tremendous support among the rank and file who are united in their particular cause, a feed cost self-sufficiency program.
I do not want to charge that the consultation process on which the Minister has embarked is a fraud. I don't want to say that, and I don't want to believe it. I would hope that the consultative process would result in meaningful changes to the legislation. But we do not see any changes, even with respect to potatoes, and that was a recommendation made by the Government of Prince Edward Island. We know what the Maritime Farmers Council is proposing. But the Minister has not acted on it. He can tell us he is going to study it, he is going to review it, but how long does the Minister need? Does he need another two years or 24 months? The Minister says he needs that much time. But he has been telling the farmers in the Maritimes that since the time the Conservatives took office.
The issue is a very serious one, Mr. Speaker. Fifty per cent of those individuals involved are on the verge of losing great sums of money as well as jobs, and all we get from this Minister is a promise that it is going to happen tomorrow or the day after, but nothing gets done. That is totally unacceptable. The Act is totally unacceptable because it does not contain the safeguards which we in the Maritime provinces want.
I heard the Hon. Member from New Brunswick speak very eloquently about this being a good first step. But that is not enough. If the Government can bail out the multinational oil companies to the tune of $1.3 billion, and if it can give $300 million of the taxpayers' money for capital gains-$600 million next year and over $1 billion in 1990-surely to God the Minister would have the courage of his convictions, and the support of his cabinet colleagues, to stand in his place tonight and announce a new program which will provide feed self-sufficiency in the Maritime provinces. But all we get from this Minister is promises, promises, promises.
